data.title: Living antiquity at Havránok
data.excerpt: On Saturday 14 July 2015 Celts, Romans, Marcomanni, Macedonians and others pitched their tents at Havránok and presented the life of antiquity to the spectators at an event organised by the Vae Victis group. Bronze casting, prehistoric weapons, a Roman field camp and a bloody offering at the sacrificial site were all part of the programme.
data.metaDescription: The Living Antiquity event at the Celtic hillfort of Havránok in 2015: Celts, Romans and Marcomanni presented the life of the period and fought battles.

mediaTexts.caption: A beauty of the Bronze Age (OZ Ipea)
mediaTexts.alt: A beauty of the Bronze Age (OZ Ipea)

children.text: things were lively from early morning on Saturday 14 July 2015. Celts, Romans, Marcomanni, Macedonians and others pitched their tents and prepared for battle. They were accompanied by their wives and children, and together in this way they presented the life of the period of antiquity to the spectators. The event was organised by the
group on premises belonging to the Liptov Museum in Ružomberok.
The civic association Ipea from the Orava region
gave us a vivid demonstration, with an engaging commentary as well, of life in the Bronze Age and above all of the casting of bronze. Others, for example

, showed weapons and tools of prehistory, or pottery and the preparation of food; the Celts the making of various tools and of items of everyday use, but also of ornaments for women and for warriors. The Romans too came in large numbers and set up their field camp here.

In between there were battles between the Celts, the Romans and warriors of other cultures, who joined both sides. In the end the Celts, together with the Romans, submitted after an indecisive battle to the will of the gods and performed a bloody offering at the sacrificial site. A wounded Celt volunteered himself, and since Taranis did not demand much blood, the armies were reconciled with one another…
Groups from Bohemia (Písek), Poland, Moravia, Austria and Slovakia took part in the event.
The fine programme was made all the more enjoyable by weather that seemed made to order, and the magical setting was a balm to the eye and to the soul.

The only thing I did not understand was the attitude of the Liptov Museum (the managers of the open-air museum). At the entrance they charged a separate admission fee, and once you had paid it you then had to pay a second time to the organisers of the event themselves. We were also outraged by the museum's attitude towards the only sellers of food and drink, who were looking after the hungry visitors. Their electricity was constantly being cut off and they were not provided with a water supply. Yet refreshments are a necessity at events like these. Visitors with children needed refreshments, and instead of making sure there was food and drink, the museum actually put obstacles in the way. An example of the narrow-minded people (the bureaucrats) of a state institution.
